segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I must boast. It does no good, but I will go on to visions and revelations of the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I know a person in Christ who fourteen years ago—whether in the body I do not know, or out of the body I do not know; God knows—was snatched up to the third heaven.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And I know that such a person—whether in the body or apart from the body I do not know; God knows—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: was snatched up into paradise and heard unutterable words, which no person is permitted to speak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On behalf of such a person I will boast, but on my own behalf I will not boast, except in my weaknesses.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if I should want to boast, I will not be a fool, for I will be speaking the truth. But I refrain, so that no one will credit me with more than what they see in me or hear from me,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: even considering how extraordinary the revelations were. Therefore, so that I would not exalt myself, a thorn in the flesh was given to me, a messenger of Satan, to beat me, so that I would not exalt myself.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: About this I pleaded with the Lord three times that it would leave me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And he has said to me,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “My grace is enough for you, for power is brought to completion in weakness.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Most gladly, then, I will rather boast in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may make its dwelling upon me.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore I am content with weaknesses, with insults, with hardships, with persecutions and distresses, for the sake of Christ; for whenever I am weak, then I am powerful.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I have become a fool; you forced me to it. For I ought to have been commended by you. For in nothing did I fall short of those super-apostles, even though I am nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The signs of an apostle were worked among you with all endurance, by signs and wonders and deeds of power.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For in what were you made worse off than the rest of the assemblies, except that I myself was not a burden to you? Forgive me this injustice!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Look, for the third time now I am ready to come to you, and I will not be a burden; for I am not seeking what is yours, but you. For children are not obliged to save up for their parents, but parents for their children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As for me, I will most gladly spend and be utterly spent for your souls. If I love you more, am I to be loved less?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But granted, I did not weigh you down; yet, crafty as I am, I caught you by deceit!

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Did I take advantage of you through any of those I have sent to you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I urged Titus to go, and I sent the brother with him. Titus did not take advantage of you, did he? Did we not walk in the same spirit? In the same footsteps?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Have you been thinking all along that we are defending ourselves to you? We are speaking before God in Christ. And all of it, beloved, is for building you up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For I fear that when I come I may somehow find you not as I wish, and that I may be found by you not as you wish; that somehow there may be strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, selfish ambition, slander, gossip, conceit, disorder.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: I fear that when I come again my God may humble me before you, and I may mourn over many of those who sinned earlier and have not turned back from the impurity and sexual immorality and debauchery that they practiced.

notes.phrase: visions and revelations of the Lord
notes.note: The Greek genitive can mean visions and revelations given by the Lord or visions and revelations in which the Lord is seen. Most interpreters take it as the first, and some translations say “from the Lord.” The English “of the Lord” leaves both open, as the Greek does.

Paul is almost certainly describing his own experience in the third person, since verse 7 treats the revelations as his; the indirection lets him report it without boasting of it. The “third heaven” reflects Jewish pictures of the heavens as layered, numbered variously as three, five or seven. Here it is probably the highest, and the same place as the “paradise” of verse 4.

The Greek adjective can mean either “impossible to put into words” or “not to be spoken,” the latter being a common term for sacred secrets. The clause that follows, about what no person is permitted to speak, favors the second sense. The Greek pairs “unspoken” with “spoken things,” a deliberate paradox that the English tries to keep.

notes.phrase: even considering how extraordinary the revelations were
notes.note: This phrase can close the sentence begun in verse 6, as here, or open the next one: “And because of the extraordinary revelations, so that I would not exalt myself…” Some manuscripts lack the word “therefore,” which makes the second reading easier. The edition translated here includes it, and so the phrase is attached to what precedes; translations are divided.

The word can mean a pointed stake, but in the Septuagint and in the ordinary Greek of the period it commonly means a thorn or splinter. What the affliction was is unknown; proposals include a chronic illness, a disability, and persecution or a particular opponent. “Messenger of Satan” could equally be translated “angel of Satan.”

“The Lord” here is most likely the risen Christ, since the reply speaks of “power” and Paul at once calls it “the power of Christ.” The reply in verse 9 is therefore marked as spoken by Jesus. A minority take “the Lord” as God the Father.

notes.phrase: power is brought to completion in weakness
notes.traditional: my strength is made perfect in weakness
notes.note: The verb means to finish, carry through or bring to its goal; “made perfect” can suggest the removal of a flaw, which is not the point. Many manuscripts read “my power,” but the earliest lack “my,” and the edition translated here omits it. The sense is little changed, since the power in view is plainly the Lord’s.

The phrase is sarcastic, built on a rare adverb meaning “exceedingly, beyond measure.” Most scholars think it refers to the rival missionaries at Corinth whom Paul attacks in chapter 11. Others think it refers to the leading apostles in Jerusalem, whose authority those rivals claimed.

The Greek is the plural of the ordinary word for “power,” the same word used in verse 9, here meaning concrete acts that display it. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and is what most translations have. “Deeds of power” is used so that the link with “power” stays visible and the word stays distinct from “signs” and “wonders.”

The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and the Septuagint’s word for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. “Assembly” is used throughout this translation to keep the first-century sense in view.

notes.phrase: crafty as I am, I caught you by deceit
notes.note: Paul is not confessing but ironically voicing a charge made against him. The accusation seems to have been that he refused support in person only to profit through his envoys and the collection. The questions in verses 17 and 18 answer that charge.

Most translations keep “repented,” an established term that readers understand to include a change of life. In current English, however, the word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek, shaped by the prophets’ call to return to God, means a change of direction in mind and conduct. “Turn back” is used for that reason.

candidates.reason: Frequent in Paul in both negative and positive senses, and translations vary among “boast,” “glory,” “take pride” and “exult,” which hides the thread running through his letters.
Used here and in 1 Thess 4:17, Acts 8:39 and Rev 12:5 for being taken up; “caught up” versus “snatched” should be decided once.
Recurs across the letters and Revelation, where translations vary among “patience,” “endurance,” “perseverance” and “steadfastness.”
Common as an address throughout the letters; “beloved,” “dear friends” and “loved ones” are all in use and should not vary from chapter to chapter.
Recurs in vice lists and in the Gospel divorce sayings; “fornication,” “sexual immorality” and “unchastity” differ noticeably in scope and tone.
